title: King's Knight Opening
description: Beat the Petrov, Philidor, and other lines. Pair this course with Italian, Scotch, Ponziani, or another opening.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/3QPB2/2N2N2/P.text:
Black attacks our queen. 

They have avoided any pin with Bb5, so we must retreat.

We'll fall back to the safe d2-square where our queen cannot be attacked.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2ppp/2np4/8/3QP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Nearly half of the games go like this: Black wants to attack our centralized queen.

We'll pin the knight and develop a piece.

r2q1rk1/1pp1bppp/p1bp1n2/8/4PB2/2NQ1N2/P.text:
Black castles as well.

We'll bring our knight to an active central square, putting pressure on the c6-bishop, and giving us the option of locating the knight on f5 where it eyes the black king's position.

r2q1rk1/1ppbbppp/p2p1n2/8/3NPB2/2NQ1P2/P.text:
We will go for a kingside pawn storm. 

g4, h4 and h5, and we'll interject the move Kb1 whenever convenient as a useful, waiting move. Black is in some trouble.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/4PB2/2N2b1P/PP.text:
Black takes.

We recapture. 

The doubled pawns are assets that will help us push in the center and attack.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/2np1n2/8/4PBb1/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black pins our knight.

We are not concerned.

We can attack the bishop and hope we get an open g-file with the bishop pair.

r2q1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/4n3/4PB2/2N1QP1P/.text:
But we can defend and threaten to take on e5. 

Our main plan is to play Bh2, f4 and e5. 

We will use the open d- and g-files to attack with our rooks, and Black will have a tough time defending.

r2q1rk1/pppbbppp/2np1n2/1B6/4PB2/2NQ1N2/.text:
Black castles.

We'll castle as well, but we'll castle on the queenside.

r2q1rk1/pppbbppp/3p1n2/1B6/1nQ1PB2/2N2N2.text:
But c4 is available to our queen. 

We will play Rhe1. 

Black's best move is now 10...Nc6, but they are unlikely to find it. One of our biggest threats is that we are planning to play e5 and expose the queen on the d-file.

r2qk2r/1pp1bppp/p1bp1n2/8/4PB2/2NQ1N2/PP.text:
Black brings their bishop out to the only available square.

We'll castle queenside.

r2qk2r/pppbbppp/2np1n2/1B6/4P3/2NQ1N2/PP.text:
Black develops the bishop to its only available square.

We'll play Bf4 and control the e5-square.

r2qkb1r/1pp2ppp/p1bp1n2/8/4P3/2NQ1N2/PPP.text:
Black develops. They have two attackers but we have two defenders.

We'll develop our bishop.

r2qkb1r/pQp2ppp/2np1n2/8/4P3/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
Taking the b7-pawn gives us massive pressure. 

10...Ne7 11.e5 gives us a large advantage.

r2qkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/1b6/1n2P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
This, for example, is a blunder.

We recapture with check, and it's a double attack.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/2np1n2/1B6/4P3/3Q1N2/PP.text:
The knight comes out to f6 and targets e4.

We'll bring our queen's knight out and support our center.

r2qkb1r/pppb1ppp/3p1n2/1B6/1n2P3/2NQ1N2/.text:
Black attacks our queen.

Qc4 is impossible here (because we lose c2). 

Therefore, we have to go to e2.

r2qkbnr/1pp2ppp/p1bp4/8/4P3/3Q1N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black recaptures, with some pressure on e4.

We'll develop our knight. 

Black's critical problem in this position is that they lack space. 

And, even worse, they won't have significant long-term pressure on our e4-pawn.

r2qkbnr/1ppb1ppp/p1np4/1B6/4P3/3Q1N2/PPP.text:
Black can play ...a6 at any moment.

Our response will be to capture on c6.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/2np4/1B6/3QP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black unpins. 

Let's be careful not to blunder the queen. There are two options: we take the knight or move away.

We'll simply move the queen back to d3.

r2qkbnr/pppb1ppp/3p4/1B6/1n2P3/3Q1N2/PPP.text:
By going to d3, we are inviting this knight attack. 

We will at times meet this attack with Qe2, and others with Qc4.

But if played right away, we should trade, as the queen is overworked by having to defend both b5 and c2.

r3k1nr/pppqbppp/8/R7/1P6/1Q6/1PP2PpP/1NB.text:
And we are very active. 

Black's best move is now ...Kf8, losing castling rights but breaking the pin.

We have interesting ways of developing like Na3 to c4.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/3p4/8/1n2P3/3Q1N2/PPP2PP.text:
The queen recaptures.

We'll move sideways to b3 where we x-ray the b7-pawn.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/8/3p4/1n2P3/1Q3N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black pushes ...d5. 

Capturing on d5 helps Black become more active.

So instead of that we'll force Black to play precisely, and attack the knight with a3.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/8/8/1P6/1Q3p2/1PP2PPP/RN.text:
They take ours.

We'll castle.

This is a wild variation that's not very likely to happen, but it illustrates the hidden dynamics in the position.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/8/8/1P6/1Q6/1PP2PpP/RNB2.text:
Black takes on g2.

We'll give a check on the open e-file.

r3kbnr/pppq1ppp/8/8/1n2p3/PQ3N2/1PP2PPP/.text:
If the knight retreats, Black simply loses the d5-pawn, so instead there is this sneaky capture and counterattack.

We'll take the knight.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/1Q6/PPP2P.text:
And this is a double attack on b7 and f7.

White is practically winning already.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/4P3/5b2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black takes on f3 to win some time to recapture on e5.

The problem with this move is that our queen gets into the game.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP1b1/5N2/PPP2.text:
About 15% of games see this move on the board. 

It's the same opening moves as the famous Opera Game played by Paul Morphy.

We can capture on e5 because we threaten to win a pawn. 

This is now following the game.

rn1qkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5Q2/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll develop and threaten checkmate in one.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/3QPB2/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black castles.

And we'll castle on the queenside.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/3p1n2/8/3QP3/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
2...d6 causes Black only to have the e7-square for their bishop, so expect to see this move at some point.

We'll develop our dark-squared bishop, preparing to castle queenside.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/8/3QP3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Nearly 25% of games feature 4...Nf6. 

If Black ever plays ...Nc6, we'll be transposing to the main line.

We'll develop our other knight.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.text:
15% of games in the database include 2...d6. 

This opening is called the Philidor Defense. 

Black defends e5 with their d-pawn.

The Philidor isn't tough to play against: all we have to do is apply central pressure with the d4 pawn break, as Black lacks central control.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.text:
About half of the games in the database go like this. 

It's natural to release the central tension between the pawns, as 3...Nc6 4.d5 is not comfortable for Black to play.

We'll recapture on d4. 

Our queen is active and our pieces have many possible squares.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
1...e5 is Black's first move.

We'll develop with Nf3 and attack the pawn. 

Now, in all other courses, we mainly see 2...Nc6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this course, we will go over several openings that Black can play after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3. 

You'll face 2...Nc6 in roughly 70-80% of your games, but in this course, we look at everything else on move two.

Let's get started with 1.e4!

r1b1kb1r/ppppqppp/2n5/3nP3/3p4/5N2/PPP1B.text: This isn't even a threat now.

Because we will trade knights and unveil the rook on the e-file. 

We have ideas of c4 and Nxd4. Our space advantage gives us an edge: +2 according to the engine. Setups with ...Nd5 are generally bad for Black.

r1b2rk1/ppppqppp/1nn5/4P3/4Q3/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
Black castles. 

Our advantage is still evident.

r1b2rk1/ppppqppp/1nn5/4P3/4Q3/2NB1N2/PPP.text:
We attack h7. 

All of our minor pieces have active roles, while Black has an inactive bishop on c8.

Besides the king, Black has another hidden weakness: the c7-pawn, which we will attack with Nb5. This is +2 according to the engine.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/4P3/4Q2P/2N1BN2/.text:
We expand on the kingside. 

We have a straightforward plan of Ng5, attacking h7. 

If ...f5, we will take exf6 en passant and keep lines open.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/1nnp4/4P3/4Q3/2N1BN2/P.text: Black challenges our center and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bppp/2nn4/8/5Q2/2N2N2/PPPB1.text:
And we'll castle queenside. We have more space, and pressure on the d-file. 

If 10...Bf5 11.g4 is a great move. 

If not, our general plan is to play Bd3, g4, and Rg1 to attack the kingside.

r1bq1rk1/ppppbppp/1nn5/4P3/4Q3/2N1BN2/PP.text:
Black castles.

We'll go to the queenside and prepare our opposite-side castling plans.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2nn4/8/5Q2/2N2N2/PPP2PP.text:
The bishop goes out to e7.

We'll prepare queenside castling.

r1bqk2r/pppp1pbp/2n4p/4P3/4Q3/2N2N1P/PPP.text:
But we have enough defenders and we aren't worried about 9...Qe7 10.Nd5. 

Black is also in serious trouble after 9...0-0 10.Bd3. White has a great position.

r1bqk2r/pppp1pbp/2n4p/4P3/4Q3/5N1P/PPP2P.text: The bishop comes out and targets e5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/1b2Q3/2N2N2/PP.text:
This pin is a bad move.

We can attack the queen with our bishop. 

The black bishop must move again to defend the queen.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/1nn5/4P3/4Q3/2N2N2/PPP2.text:
Black develops their bishop to enable castling.

We should do the same.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2nn4/8/3Q4/2N2N2/PPP2PP.text:
They develop and attack our queen.

Our queen will be safe on f4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1p1p/2n4p/4P3/3Q4/5N1P/PPP2.text:
Black attacks our queen.

And we'll bring the queen to the strong central square, e4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/1nn5/4P3/3Q4/2N2N2/PPP.text:
In this variation, Black can play ...Nc6.

But their position is still bad because they lack space and we have a powerful pawn on e5 that cannot be challenged because our queen is on e4.

rn2kb1r/ppp1qppp/2npb3/5P2/3N4/2N5/PPP1B.text:
Black can't defend everything. 

We are completely winning now and will emerge up material one way or another. 

10...Bd7 11.Nd5 and Black is in huge trouble.

rn2kb1r/ppp1qppp/2npb3/8/3N1P2/2N5/PPP1B.text: The knight goes to c6 and offers a trade.

rn2kb1r/ppp1qppp/3pb3/4n3/3N4/2N5/PPP1BP.text:
Black defends.

We now have the powerful move f4. This seeks to attack the bishop and interrupt its defensive role.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/1qp5/3nP3/2BQ4/5N2/PPP.text:
Black proposes a queen trade.

Exchanging minor pieces first is good, because we create a weakness on d5.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/2p5/q2nP3/2BQ4/5N2/PPP.text:
Some may be tempted to play this check.

But we can block with a tempo on the queen.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/3pP3/3N4/2N5/PPPB1PP.text:
This is nearly +3 for us. 

We have the c7-square to attack and Black's d5-pawn is also in a lot of trouble.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/8/3pP3/3N4/8/PPPB1PPP/.text:
And Black recaptures. 

Besides a weakness on d5, we get access to the b5-square.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/1npq4/8/3Q4/1B3N2/PPP2PP.text:
We castle. 

We will play Re1 and Nxd4 if the queen trade happens.

Nc3 is also a good move and we have pressure along the e-file.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1qppp/3p4/4n3/3N4/8/PPP1BPPP.text:
Black wants to develop the light-squared bishop.

We'll develop our other knight and threaten to attack the queen with Nd5.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/5n2/4P3/3p4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Almost 25% of the time, 4...Qe7 is played.

5.Be2 is multi-purpose: we unpin and get ready to castle. 

We also threaten the knight.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/3nP3/3p4/5N2/PPP1BPP.text:
5...Nd5 once again puts the knight on a bad square.

We'll castle. Our rook is coming to e1 so our e5-pawn won't be able to be taken.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/4P3/3p2n1/5N2/PPP1BP.text:
Black can go after our pawn.

We don't mind if they take on e5 because we get good play. 

Sometimes with Re1, elsewhere with f4, as we'll see here.

rnb1kb1r/ppppqppp/8/4n3/3p4/5N2/PPP1BPPP.text:
Black takes our pawn.

And we'll take on d4.

rnbq1Bk1/pp1pbp1p/1np3p1/4P3/6Q1/1B3N2/P.text: But we now win material. This position should not prove too difficult to convert.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pbp1p/1np3pB/4P3/6Q1/1B3N2/P.text: The pawn is pushed forward to protect against checkmate.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pbppp/1np5/4P3/6Q1/1B3N2/PPP.text:
Castling saves the g7-pawn.

But we have Bh6! Now Black must give up the exchange.

rnbqk2r/pp1pbppp/1np5/4P3/3Q4/1B3N2/PPP2.text:
Passive development will surely be losing for Black.

Even now, we can begin to attack some pawns thanks to our active pieces. Qg4 targets the black kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/1np5/4P3/2BQ4/5N2/PPP2.text:
The knight goes to b6 and attacks our bishop.

But b3 is a great square for the bishop. 

Normal developing moves won't cut it for Black. They need to play actively with ...d5 at some point.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/2p5/3nP3/3Q4/5N2/PPP2P.text:
More than half of the games continue with 5...c6. 

Black defends their knight and hopes to keep it active on the center. 

The downside is ...Nc6 cannot be played anymore.

We can develop our bishop and attack the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/1np5/3pP3/3Q4/1B3N2/PPP2.text:
7...d5 is the correct move, staking a claim to the center.

Here we will take en passant.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3n4/8/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.text:
But Black recaptures. 

This line is solid because Black has dealt with our central e5-pawn.

We'll develop with Nc3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/3Qn3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Black has 5...d5 to support the knight.

We must take en passant because we don't want the knight to stay on e4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/7p/4P3/3p4/5N1P/PPP2PP.text:
The pawn recaptures.

We'll take the central d4-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/1n6/4P3/3Q4/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
A third of games include this retreat.

We should develop our other knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
This is the Petrov's Defense. 

The database says roughly 12% of games go like this.

Black counterattacks our pawn on e4. This opening is considered solid at the highest level.

I would recommend that you push d4. 

We present Black with two main choices. They either take on e4 or on d4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Almost half of the games see this move on the board. 

Black takes on d4. 

Without e5, this variation would be bad.

But when we do play e5, attacking the knight this early causes Black to become destabilized.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/7n/4P3/3p4/5N1P/PPP2PP.text:
This retreat is forced.

Now we can destroy Black's structure.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/3nP3/3p4/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
The most popular move is 4...Nd5. 

It's played almost 30% of the time, probably because it looks like a safe, centralized square for the knight.

But the knight's safety can quickly disappear, and that's why 4...Nd5 is a bad move. We'll take on d4 with our queen, and the knight finds itself attacked once more.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/3p2n1/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
4...Ng4 attacks our pawn. 

It's the third most popular, but it's also a borderline losing move.

h3 gives us the advantage. 

The knight has to move away and it will no longer be attacking our pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/3pn3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
This is the top computer and master-level move. 

Black centralizes their knight. 

It isn't so easy to displace it.

We can take on d4 and attack it.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black plays 1...e5.

We'll develop and attack e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The database has more than 100 million games in the Petrov's Defense. 

Though you are more likely to see other openings, it's still important to be prepared to face this opening. 

In this study, we will analyze our main line against it.

We'll begin with 1.e4.

r1b1kb1r/p1p2ppp/2p5/2n1P3/8/2N2N2/PPP2P.text:
And we bring the knight out. 

We should develop our dark-squared bishop and castle queenside. 

It should be an easy endgame to play, up a pawn, and with Black's queenside pawns compromised.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/2nBP3/8/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
Not only do we win a pawn, but we can also damage Black's pawn structure.

We'll take the knight which was attacking our e5-pawn.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3qP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Black has no choice but to trade queens.

We'll recapture, attacking the e4-knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pb4/3pN3/2PP1P2/2PB4/.text:
If they trade, we will have a mighty pawn chain pointing at their kingside, facilitating our attack.

We also have Qh5 ideas to attack h7. We have a small edge, but with the attack it shouldn't be easy for Black to hold.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pb4/3pN3/2PP4/2PB4/P4.text:
Black can challenge our knight. 

However, we are here prepared to stand our ground.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP.text: Black may try to attack f2.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bQP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP.text:
But we have a winning tactic. 

6.Qd5 is a double attack, hitting the e4-knight and threatening mate on f7.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3pP3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2.text:
5...d5 is an attempt to complicate matters.

En passant would be a big mistake here, losing our entire advantage. We should simply take the pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/8/3pN3/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PP.text:
This occurs in about 15% of games. 

Our knight is challenged right away.

We should simply accept the trade.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP.text:
The third most popular move, played approximately 10% of the time, is 3...Nc6.

It's not a good move because we can take on e5.

This comes with a tempo on the f6-knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/4n3/5N2/PPP2PP.text:
Black can take our pawn. 

Their problem is that our e5-pawn is strong and the knight on e4 isn't stable.

We can set up some Bxf7+ or Qd5 tactics.

For example, 5...d6 simply results in 6.Bxf7+ followed by Qd5+.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/2pb4/3p4/2PPn3/2NB4/PP3P.text:
And we create tension between our knights and on the d5-pawn. 

Black can deal with our threats soundly with ...Nxc3 at any moment, but I like our positional edge after cxd5 because we'll create an IQP (isolated queen's pawn) to fight against.

r2qk2r/pppb1ppp/3b4/3p4/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PPP.text:
In a perfect world, Black would lose time with a move like 7...a6, and we would attack with 8.c4 and 
Re1.

But instead, Black realizes they have to get the king out of the center.

c4 is still the way forward for us, undermining the defender of the central knight.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p5/3pP3/2P1n3/3B4/PP3PP.text:
This is always Black's safe option.

Now 9.Qc2 creates pressure on h7.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb4/3pN3/2PPn3/3B4/PP3P.text:
Black defends the d5-pawn.

We'll develop our knight and propose a trade. 

This also adds some pressure to d5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb4/4N3/2pP4/2PB4/P4PPP.text:
Black can also take on c4. 

This gives up their central control.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb4/8/2NP4/2PB4/P4PPP/R.text:
We have more space and central control. 

We will play Nxd6 if possible, and a4 with Ba3. We have a considerable advantage.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2p5/3PPp2/4n3/3B4/PPQ2PPP.text:
10...Qxd5 blunders the queen. Can you see how? 

With this move, we control the c5-square, preventing ...Nc5 and we will play f3 after Black recaptures on d5 with the c-pawn.

Our knight is coming to c3 and Black is going to find it very difficult to hang on to the isolated d-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/2p5/3pPp2/2P1n3/3B4/PPQ2P.text: Overprotecting the knight does not work.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b4/3pN3/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2P.text:
Most people don't give up the bishop and just castle.

We should play to undermine the d5-pawn. 

This is one of the key pawn breaks in this opening.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/8/2nPP3/8/3B4/PP3PPP/RN.text:
But that's a free pawn. 

It cannot be recaptured because of discovered check tactics. We should convert this without problems.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/8/2npP3/2P5/3B4/PP3PPP/.text: The knight jumps away and attacks our bishop.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/8/3pP3/4n3/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black castles.

Our c4 idea works in this line, too. 

The point is to undermine the knight's defender.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3b4/3pN3/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PP.text:
Black could apply pressure to our knight with their bishop.

But if they want to take with their bishop and give up the bishop pair, we'll allow it.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/8/3pb3/3Pn3/3B4/PPP2PPP/.text:
You may see some players take on e5. 

We like this!

We get the powerful bishop pair and a strong pawn on e5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.text:
Less than 10% of games continue like this. 

Black simply defends e5.

We'll take. 

This move will give us a favorable queen trade if Black recaptures the e5-pawn. 4...dxe5 happens half the time here, actually!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/2B1n3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
We have the tricky 5.Bc4, with a healthy advantage. 

Some popular continuations that make up nearly half of the games are 5...dxe5 and 5...Bg4, both of which are losing. 

If 5...dxe5 6.Qxd8+ and we will play Nxe5, hitting f7.

If 5...Bg4 6.Qd5 and we're attacking e4, b7 and f7!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p4/4P3/4n3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text: The other half of the games goes like this: Black takes the pawn on e4, which is the best move.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/3Pn3/3B1N2/PPP2P.text:
Black defends their knight.

We can now centralize our knight and get our pawn back.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black attacks our pawn.

And we'll go for the central pawn break.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/3Pn3/5N2/PPP2PPP.text:
This is the second most popular move, found in about 27% of the games, but it's the most played amongst master-level players.

We can get a balanced game, but our moves are more natural. 

Here we will develop and attack a piece.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black mirrors us.

We'll develop and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
To complete this chapter, I want us to look at some other Petrov's Defense variations.

Of highest importance is the move 3...Nxe4, played by masters.

We'll begin with 1.e4.

lessons.title: Black Plays 2...Bc5, Qf6, d5 and f5

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3Pq3/4BN2/PPP2.text:
We block, and the bishop is now under attack. 

This position is nearly +2 for us. 

We will play Nc3 if ...Bb6 or c3 if ...Bb4+. Black's queen will get kicked around and we'll develop our pieces quickly.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/3Pq3/5N2/PPP2P.text: Black takes. They win back their pawn, but their position is bad.

r1b1k1nr/ppppqppp/2n5/2b5/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
The queen attacks e4.

We should attack the bishop and let Black take on e4.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4q3/2B1p3/2N5/PPP2P.text:
The queen recaptures.

We'll offer a knight trade on d5.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4qP2/2B5/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
And now we take on f5. 

Black is in some trouble. They have allowed us an open position against their king. 

We will play Nc3 and Re1. Simple moves that pack a big punch.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4qp2/2B1P3/8/PPP2PP.text: The black queen moves yet again.

r1b1kb1r/pppp2pp/8/3Bq3/4p3/8/PPP2PPP/R1.text:
We will take on e4 next.

After that, we can go Qd3 to attack h7, or g3 defensively if we want to to play Bf4 and Bg2 later.

r1b1kb1r/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/4N3/2BPp3/8/PPP2.text:
Black takes on e4 with the f-pawn.

We'll develop our knight. 

Even though Black gave up a pawn for activity, it is White who is getting all the developed pieces.

r1b1kb1r/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/4Np2/2BPP3/8/PPP.text:
Black can also choose to develop the knight.

This is an attack on our knight but we can ignore it.

We will simply castle. 

Black wanted e-file counterplay, but very soon it will be White who will have it.

r1b1kb1r/ppppq1pp/5n2/4np2/2BPP3/8/PPP2P.text:
If Black trades, we are fine with this.

We will recapture with a tempo on the f6-knight.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1P.text:
Black could also try to get a knight trade with the idea of opening up lines.

We can refuse and keep our knight near our king, defending key squares.

rn2kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3q1b2/4p3/3P1N2/PPPN.text:
Black defends again.

We'll take. 

Black is practically lost.

rn2kb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3q1b2/4n2N/8/PPPNQPPP/.text:
A very simple idea: we attack the defender on f5 and f3 is also next.

We will emerge up material.

rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/1b6/4N3/3Pq3/4B3/PPP2P.text:
The bishop goes to b6.

We will develop and attack the queen.

rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/1b6/4Nq2/2BP4/4B3/PPPN.text: This gambit, which has led to a position where we are many tempi up in development and the computer gives us +3, should not be an issue.

rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/1b6/4Nq2/3P4/4B3/PPPN1.text:
The queen goes to f5. 

It's not on an active square here, and most of Black's pieces are on the 8th rank.

rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1N3/3Pq3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
Black takes with check.

We'll block with Be3.

Black's big problem will be development.

A fun fact: the second most popular move is 5...Bxd4 here. It seems many players at low Elo miss that the pawn is defended!

rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1N3/4P2q/8/PPPP1PP.text:
The idea is to attack f2 and e4.

We can give the e-pawn back. 

The point of d4 is that it accelerates our development.

rnb1kb1r/ppp1q1pp/3p1n2/4Np2/2BPP3/8/PPP.text:
Black's direct approach is to go after our e-pawn.

But this is wrong because it neglects development.

We will attack the rook on h8.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2Npp/3p1n2/5p2/2BPq3/8/PPP2P.text:
But it's only a check. 

We have a threat on the rook and we'll also create threats on the queen next. 

This is +3.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3q4/4p3/3P1N2/PPP1Q.text:
Most games continue with 5...Qxd5.

We can develop and increase pressure on the pawn.

rnb1kb1r/pppp1qpp/5n2/8/4p3/2N1N3/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops and defends e4.

Firstly, we will dislodge the queen from the comfortable f7 square.

rnb1kb1r/pppp2pp/5nq1/8/2B1p3/2NPN3/PPP2.text: Finally! And we enjoy a great position. Next we will trade and castle before making advances into Black's territory.

rnb1kb1r/ppppq1pp/5n2/4Np2/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.text:
Black wants e-file play, but we shouldn't panic.

We've got 5.d4 to defend our knight and to activate our dark-squared bishop at some point.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1ppp/2p2q2/4p3/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black knows they have to stop that move.

But we can go for an attack on e5 and prepare Bg5. We'll strike in the center with d4.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1ppp/2p2q2/8/3pP3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
Black trades in the center.

And we attack the queen.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1ppp/2p3q1/6B1/3QP3/2N2N2/P.text:
We're completely winning. Four pieces developed and a central pawn. 

Black has lost too much time with the queen.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1ppp/2p3q1/6B1/3pP3/2N2N2/P.text:
Black moves away to g6.

They are no longer defending d4.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1qpp/2p5/8/4p3/2N1N3/PPPP1P.text:
If 6...c6, we cannot play Bc4 because we run into their move d5.

Instead, 7.d3 is the way.

We'll undermine their most advanced pawn.

rnb1kbnr/pp1p1qpp/2p5/8/8/2NBN3/PPP2PPP/.text:
And we recapture with our bishop. 

We have three developed minor pieces to Black's zero. We'll be playing 0-0 and Re1 next and attacking the exposed king.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1ppp/5q2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
2...Qf6 is 2% of games.

The queen is out, in contradiction to basic opening principles.

We should aim to attack it with Nd5.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.text:
This is a super tricky defensive move, but we're fine.

We'll retreat the knight, covering the important d5 square. d3 is very much in our plans.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
Black attacks our knight.

We'll move away.

Our plan is Nc3, Ne3, and in many positions Bc4 with d3.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.text:
Black captures, which happens in roughly 80% of games.

We'll develop and attack the pawn on e4.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/6q1/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.text:
Black doesn't have an easy way of defending, so most often plays like this.

We undermine e4... but it looks like we made a mistake!

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/6q1/8/2N5/2Np4/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black captures. Surely we cannot recapture with the bishop?

But we can!

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/8/7Q/2N5/2NB4/PPP2PqP/R.text: Oops! Next, we have either Qe5+ and/or Be4, winning on the spot.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/8/8/2N5/2NB4/PPP2PqP/R1.text: Seen in 72% of games. And now...

rnb1kbr1/ppp1qNpp/3p1n2/5p2/2BPP3/2N5/PP.text:
We'll castle next and play Re1. 

There will be no way for Black to defend everything. Again, this is winning according to the engine.

rnb1kbr1/ppp1qNpp/3p1n2/5p2/2BPP3/8/PPP2.text: The rook moves away from danger.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2bP4/4P3/2P2N2/PP2Q.text:
The bishop moves away to c5.

We can develop and pin the black knight with Bg5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3P4/1b2p3/2PP1N2/PP.text:
Black castles, unpinning the e-pawn. Now our knight is attacked.

We'll take it and suddenly have a massive pawn formation in the center.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
This is the Busch-Gass Gambit. 

While it's only 3% of games, there are more than 27 million games in this variation.

The gambit isn't good at all, though. 

We can simply take the pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3P4/1b2p3/3P1N2/PPP1.text:
This is one of Black's options: they're hoping we make a mistake with Nc3.

But we can win yet another tempo with c3.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3P4/4p3/5N2/PPPPQPP.text:
Black defends their pawn.

And we'll attack it further.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.text:
This move is also played a lot. Black prioritizes development.

We will focus on attacking the f7-square and creating counterplay.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/4p3/5N2/PPPP1PPP/.text:
The dynamic aspect of the gambit. 

We take a pawn, but they push theirs and attack us.

However, the Qe2 line is known to be good.

We attack e4 and pin the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
This is called the Elephant Gambit.

It's seen in about 2% of games played.

We should accept and take on d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
Black plays 1...e5.

We'll develop and attack the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.text:
This is the Latvian Gambit. It's a decent weapon with plenty of traps.

We'll take on e5 and go for a simple approach.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Finally, I want to show you some gambits and deviations on move 2 that you may encounter as a 1.e4 e5 player.

We'll begin with 1.e4.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/2bP2B1/4P3/2P2N2/PP.text:
Our knight simply defends. 

This is +2 for us. We have two extra central pawns and the f6-knight is pinned.
If Black puts more pressure on our center...
